items.title: Focus Question: Why do power companies send electricity over long lines at very high potential difference, and what do transformers do? Use a 2.0-MW plant and a line of total resistance 5.0 𝛺 to compare 20 kV with 200 kV

body.html: 𝑃= 2.0 × 10<sup>6</sup> W, 𝑅<sub>line</sub> = 5.0 𝛺, 𝑉<sub>1</sub> = 2.0 × 10<sup>4</sup> V, 𝑉<sub>2</sub> = 2.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> V. Unknown: line current and power lost for each case.
The line current is 𝐼= 𝑃/ 𝑉 and the power wasted as heat in the line is 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅.
𝐼<sub>1</sub> = 𝑃 𝑉<sub>1</sub> = 2.0 × 10<sup>6</sup> W 2.0 × 10<sup>4</sup> V
𝐼<sub>2</sub> = 2.0 × 10<sup>6</sup> W

answer.html: A step-up transformer at the plant raises the potential difference, which lowers the current in the line. At 20 kV the line wastes 50 kW; at 200 kV it wastes only 0.50 kW, one hundredth as much. Step-down transformers near homes then lower the potential difference to a safe level.

check.html: Raising the potential difference 10 times lowers the current 10 times and the 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅 loss 100 times.

items.title: Figure 10 (Apply): A bar magnet is held with its north pole facing a coil and is pulled away. How does the force on the coil compare with the case when the magnet approaches, and in which direction is the induced current as seen from the magnet?

body.html: Lenz's law: the induced field opposes the change. Counterclockwise current seen from a face makes that face a north pole.

The north pole of the magnet faces the coil, and the field through the coil points toward the coil. It is decreasing as the magnet retreats. The coil must make a field in the same direction to oppose the decrease, so its near face becomes a south pole. A south pole faces the magnet's north pole, so they attract. For the near face to be a south pole, the current must be clockwise as seen from the magnet.

answer.html: The force on the coil is attractive: the coil is pulled after the retreating magnet, resisting the change. The induced current is clockwise as seen from the magnet's side.

check.html: If the force were repulsive, pulling the magnet away would be easier and the magnet would gain energy for free, violating energy conservation.

items.title: Crosscutting Concepts: Cause and Effect (a table saw motor in a workshop)

answer.html: Cause: starting a table saw makes the motor draw a large current, because there is no opposing induced EMF until the blade turns. Effects: (1) The large current produces a bigger potential drop in the supply wires, so lights on the same circuit dim for a moment. (2) Once the blade is up to speed, the induced EMF opposes the current, and the current falls. (3) If the blade jams or the wood binds, the motor slows, the opposing EMF drops, the current rises, and the wires and motor can overheat. (4) Switching off suddenly can produce a spark at the switch. Safety precautions: use properly rated breakers and wire, never force a stalled blade, switch off and let the motor stop before clearing a jam, and do not overload the circuit with other tools. The evidence is each statement in the Lenz's law discussion (starting current, load, dimming lights, sparks).

check.html: Each safety rule follows from one of the cause-and-effect links.

items.title: Get It?: A phone charger plugged into a 120-V outlet delivers 5.0 V. Is its transformer step-up or step-down, and how do the turns and the currents compare?

body.html: 𝑉<sub>𝑠</sub>/ 𝑉<sub>𝑝</sub>= 𝑁<sub>𝑠</sub>/ 𝑁<sub>𝑝</sub> and, for an ideal transformer, 𝑉<sub>𝑝</sub>𝐼<sub>𝑝</sub>= 𝑉<sub>𝑠</sub>𝐼<sub>𝑠</sub>.
The secondary potential difference is lower than the primary, so 𝑁<sub>𝑠</sub>< 𝑁<sub>𝑝</sub>. If the primary has 𝑁<sub>𝑝</sub>= 2400 turns:

answer.html: It is a step-down transformer. The secondary has fewer turns (100 compared with 2400) and carries 24 times the current of the primary.

check.html: The power is the same on both sides (ideally), so lower potential difference means higher current.

items.title: 16 (Lesson 2, Practice): A step-down transformer has 6000 primary turns and 150 secondary turns. The primary potential difference is 8.4 kV and the secondary current is 28 A. Find 𝑉𝑠 and 𝐼𝑝

body.html: 𝑁<sub>𝑝</sub>= 6000, 𝑁<sub>𝑠</sub>= 150, 𝑉<sub>𝑝</sub>= 8.4 × 10<sup>3</sup> V, 𝐼<sub>𝑠</sub>= 28 A. Unknown: 𝑉<sub>𝑠</sub>, 𝐼<sub>𝑝</sub>.
The potential difference is proportional to the turns, 𝑉<sub>𝑝</sub>/ 𝑉<sub>𝑠</sub>= 𝑁<sub>𝑝</sub>/ 𝑁<sub>𝑠</sub>. For an ideal transformer, 𝑉<sub>𝑝</sub>𝐼<sub>𝑝</sub>= 𝑉<sub>𝑠</sub>𝐼<sub>𝑠</sub>.

answer.html: 𝑉<sub>𝑠</sub>= 2.1 × 10<sup>2</sup> V; 𝐼<sub>𝑝</sub>= 0.70 A

items.title: 17 (Lesson 2, Challenge): A 92-percent-efficient step-up transformer has 250 primary turns and 4500 secondary turns. The primary potential difference is 48.0 V and the secondary current is 0.80 A. Find 𝑉𝑠 and 𝐼𝑝

body.html: 𝑁<sub>𝑝</sub>= 250, 𝑁<sub>𝑠</sub>= 4500, 𝑉<sub>𝑝</sub>= 48.0 V, efficiency = 0.92, 𝐼<sub>𝑠</sub>= 0.80 A. Unknown: 𝑉<sub>𝑠</sub>, 𝐼<sub>𝑝</sub>.
The turns ratio still sets the potential differences, 𝑉<sub>𝑠</sub>= 𝑉<sub>𝑝</sub>(𝑁<sub>𝑠</sub>/ 𝑁<sub>𝑝</sub>). Efficiency is output power over input power, so 𝑃<sub>𝑝</sub>= 𝑃<sub>𝑠</sub>/ 0.92.

answer.html: 𝑉<sub>𝑠</sub>= 8.6 × 10<sup>2</sup> V; 𝐼<sub>𝑝</sub>≈16 A

check.html: An ideal transformer would need 14.4 A; the real one needs slightly more because of thermal losses.

items.title: 18 (Check Your Progress): A closed aluminum ring hangs from a thread beside a bar magnet. The south pole of the magnet is pulled away from the ring. Which way does the ring swing? What if the ring has a gap cut in it?

answer.html: The ring swings toward the magnet, following the direction the magnet is moving. The retreating south pole decreases the field through the ring, so by Lenz's law the induced current makes a field that opposes the decrease. The ring's near face becomes a north pole, which attracts the magnet's south pole, so the ring is pulled after the magnet. If the ring has a gap, no current can flow, so no magnetic force is produced and the ring does not swing.

check.html: In both cases the ring's motion tends to oppose the change, which is Lenz's law.

items.title: 19 (Check Your Progress): Why is a spark more likely when you unplug a running blender than when you unplug a toaster?

answer.html: A blender has a motor with many coils that carry a current and create a strong magnetic field. When the plug is pulled, the current and the field fall suddenly. The changing field induces a large EMF (self-inductance) in the direction that tries to keep the current going, and it can be large enough to jump a spark. A toaster element is essentially just a resistor, with little magnetic field and negligible self-inductance, so no large EMF appears.

check.html: The effect grows with how fast the current is cut off.

items.title: 20 (Check Your Progress): A student connects the primary of a transformer to a steady 9-V battery. The lamp on the secondary stays off. When the switch is first closed, the lamp flashes briefly. Explain both observations

answer.html: A transformer works by mutual inductance, which needs a changing magnetic field in the core. A battery gives a steady current, so after the first instant the field in the core is constant, and no EMF is induced in the secondary and the lamp stays off. While the current is rising from zero at the moment the switch closes, the field changes, so a brief EMF is induced and the lamp flashes. It would flash again briefly when the switch opens. AC gives a continuously changing field and so a continuous output.

check.html: Faraday's law: no change in field, no induced EMF.

items.title: 21 (Check Your Progress): A welding transformer has a primary of 240 V carrying 6.0 A and a secondary of 30 V. Find the secondary current. Which coil should be made of thicker wire, and why?

body.html: For an ideal transformer, 𝑉<sub>𝑝</sub>𝐼<sub>𝑝</sub>= 𝑉<sub>𝑠</sub>𝐼<sub>𝑠</sub>. Heating of the wire is 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅.

answer.html: 𝐼<sub>𝑠</sub>= 48 A. The secondary (few turns, low potential difference) carries the larger current and needs thick, low-resistance wire so it does not overheat (𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅). The primary has more turns and a smaller current, so thinner wire is enough, and thin wire lets many turns fit on the core.

check.html: The current ratio 48 / 6.0 = 8 matches the potential difference ratio 240 / 30 = 8.

items.title: 22 (Check Your Progress): The secondary of a step-down doorbell transformer (turns ratio 𝑁𝑝/ 𝑁𝑠= 10) is accidentally short-circuited. What happens to the primary current? Its secondary current rises from 0.50 A to 8.0 A; find the primary current before and after

body.html: For an ideal transformer, 𝑉<sub>𝑝</sub>𝐼<sub>𝑝</sub>= 𝑉<sub>𝑠</sub>𝐼<sub>𝑠</sub> and 𝑉<sub>𝑝</sub>/ 𝑉<sub>𝑠</sub>= 𝑁<sub>𝑝</sub>/ 𝑁<sub>𝑠</sub>, so 𝐼<sub>𝑝</sub>= 𝐼<sub>𝑠</sub>(𝑁<sub>𝑠</sub>/ 𝑁<sub>𝑝</sub>).

answer.html: The primary current rises as well, from 0.050 A to 0.80 A, which is 16 times larger. The short circuit has almost no resistance, so the secondary current becomes very large, and the primary must supply that power. The large currents can overheat the windings or blow a fuse.

check.html: The ratio of currents, 0.80 / 0.050 = 16, equals the ratio of secondary currents, 8.0 / 0.50 = 16 .

items.title: 23 (Check Your Progress, Critical Thinking): A student wants to build a transformer with a wooden core because wood is cheap and does not conduct electricity. Would it work as well as iron?

answer.html: No. Wood is not magnetic, so it does not concentrate the magnetic field made by the primary. Most of the field would spread out into the air and little of it would pass through the secondary coil, so the induced EMF would be small and the transformer would waste energy. A soft iron core is easily magnetized, strengthens the field, and guides it through both coils, so almost all of the changing flux links the primary and secondary.

check.html: The core's job is to concentrate and carry the changing flux from primary to secondary.

items.title: Focus Question: How do transformers help with the distribution of electricity in the power grid?

answer.html: Step-up transformers at the power plant raise the potential difference (up to about 480, 000 V), which lowers the current in the long transmission lines (𝑃= 𝑉𝐼), so less energy is wasted as heat (𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅). Step-down transformers near homes then reduce the potential difference to a safe 120 V for use.

items.title: Figure 10 (Apply): How would the force on the coil change if the magnet's south pole faced the coil?

body.html: Lenz's law: the induced field opposes the change, so the coil always pushes back against the approaching magnet.

With the south pole approaching, the field through the coil points toward the magnet and is increasing. The coil must create a field pointing away from the magnet, so the coil's near face becomes a south pole, facing the magnet's south pole. The induced current therefore flows in the opposite direction (clockwise instead of counterclockwise when viewed from the same side). Like poles still face each other, so the force is still repulsive.

answer.html: The force on the coil would not change in direction or size: it is still a repulsive push away from the approaching magnet. Only the direction of the induced current reverses.

check.html: If the force were attractive, the magnet would speed up and gain energy for free, violating energy conservation.

items.title: Crosscutting Concepts: Cause and Effect (motors in the household)

answer.html: Cause: starting a motor makes it draw a large current, because there is no opposing induced EMF until it turns. Effects: (1) The large current produces a bigger potential drop across the resistance of the supply wires, so other devices in parallel (such as lightbulbs) get a lower potential difference and dim. (2) Once the motor turns, an induced EMF opposes the current, so the current falls. (3) If a load slows or stalls the motor, the opposing EMF drops, the current rises, and the wires and motor can overheat. (4) Interrupting the current makes the collapsing field induce a large EMF that can make a spark. Safety precautions: do not stall or overload a motor, use correctly rated fuses or breakers and wire gauge, do not run a motor on an overloaded circuit, keep switches and plugs away from flammable materials, and switch off and let the motor stop before clearing a jam. The evidence is each statement in the Lenz's law section above (starting current, load, dimming lights, sparking).

check.html: Each safety rule follows from one of the cause-and-effect links.

items.title: Get It?: How do step-up transformers differ from step-down transformers?

answer.html: A step-up transformer has more turns on the secondary than on the primary (𝑁<sub>𝑠</sub>> 𝑁<sub>𝑝</sub>), so 𝑉<sub>𝑠</sub>> 𝑉<sub>𝑝</sub> and 𝐼<sub>𝑠</sub>< 𝐼<sub>𝑝</sub>. A step-down transformer has fewer secondary turns (𝑁<sub>𝑠</sub>< 𝑁<sub>𝑝</sub>), so 𝑉<sub>𝑠</sub>< 𝑉<sub>𝑝</sub> and 𝐼<sub>𝑠</sub>> 𝐼<sub>𝑝</sub>. Power is the same on both sides (ideally).

check.html: Matches the "Connecting Math to Physics" table in the book.

items.title: 16 (Lesson 2, Practice): Step-down transformer, 7500 primary turns, 125 secondary turns, 𝑉𝑝= 7.2 kV, 𝐼𝑠= 36 A

body.html: 𝑁<sub>𝑝</sub>= 7500, 𝑁<sub>𝑠</sub>= 125, 𝑉<sub>𝑝</sub>= 7.2 × 10<sup>3</sup> V, 𝐼<sub>𝑠</sub>= 36 A. Unknown: 𝑉<sub>𝑠</sub>, 𝐼<sub>𝑝</sub>.

The potential difference is proportional to the turns, 𝑉<sub>𝑝</sub>/ 𝑉<sub>𝑠</sub>= 𝑁<sub>𝑝</sub>/ 𝑁<sub>𝑠</sub>. For an ideal transformer, power is equal on both sides, 𝑉<sub>𝑝</sub>𝐼<sub>𝑝</sub>= 𝑉<sub>𝑠</sub>𝐼<sub>𝑠</sub>.

answer.html: 𝑉<sub>𝑠</sub>= 1.2 × 10<sup>2</sup> V; 𝐼<sub>𝑝</sub>= 0.60 A

items.title: 17 (Lesson 2, Challenge): 95-percent-efficient step-up transformer, 300 and 90,000 turns, 𝑉𝑝= 60.0 V, 𝐼𝑠= 0.50 A

body.html: 𝑁<sub>𝑝</sub>= 300, 𝑁<sub>𝑠</sub>= 90, 000, 𝑉<sub>𝑝</sub>= 60.0 V, efficiency = 0.95, 𝐼<sub>𝑠</sub>= 0.50 A. Unknown: 𝑉<sub>𝑠</sub>, 𝐼<sub>𝑝</sub>.
The turns ratio still sets the voltages, 𝑉<sub>𝑠</sub>= 𝑉<sub>𝑝</sub>(𝑁<sub>𝑠</sub>/ 𝑁<sub>𝑝</sub>). The efficiency is output power over input power, so 𝑃<sub>𝑝</sub>= 𝑃<sub>𝑠</sub>/ 0.95.

check.html: An ideal transformer would need 150 A; the real one needs slightly more because of the thermal losses.

items.title: 18 (Check Your Progress): A hanging coil with its ends joined; a magnet is plunged into it. Which way does it swing?

answer.html: The coil swings away from the magnet, in the direction the magnet is moving. The approaching magnet increases the field through the coil, so by Lenz's law the induced current makes a field that opposes the increase. This makes the coil's near face the same pole as the magnet's approaching pole, so the two repel, and the repulsion pushes the coil away. (If the magnet were pulled out, the coil would be attracted and swing after it.)

check.html: In both cases the coil's motion tends to oppose the change, which is Lenz's law.

items.title: 19 (Check Your Progress): Why is a spark more likely when unplugging a running vacuum cleaner than a lit lamp?

answer.html: A motor has many coils with a strong magnetic field while it carries current. When the plug is pulled, the current falls suddenly and so does the magnetic field. The changing field induces a large EMF (self-inductance) in a direction that tries to keep the current going, and this EMF can be large enough to jump a spark across the plug and outlet. A lamp filament is essentially just a resistor, with little magnetic field and negligible self-inductance, so no large EMF is induced.

check.html: The effect grows with the rate at which the current is cut off.

items.title: 20 (Check Your Progress): Why may a transformer be operated only on AC?

answer.html: A transformer works by mutual inductance, which needs a changing magnetic field in the core to induce an EMF in the secondary. AC produces a continuously changing field. DC produces a steady field once the current is constant, so there is no change and no induced EMF in the secondary (except for a brief moment when the DC is switched on or off). A DC supply could also overheat the primary, whose only limit on current is its small resistance.

check.html: Faraday's law: no change in field, no induced EMF.

items.title: 21 (Check Your Progress): Why are coils with few turns made of thick wire and coils with many turns of thin wire?

answer.html: In a transformer, 𝑉<sub>𝑝</sub>𝐼<sub>𝑝</sub>= 𝑉<sub>𝑠</sub>𝐼<sub>𝑠</sub>. The coil with few turns has the lower potential difference and so carries the larger current. Large currents heat a wire by 𝐼<sup>2</sup>𝑅, so this coil needs a low- resistance (thick) wire to avoid overheating and energy loss. The many-turn coil has a high potential difference and a small current, so thin wire is enough, and thin wire lets many turns fit on the core.

check.html: In Example Problem 2, the 200-turn coil carries 30 A and the 3000-turn coil only 2.0 A.

items.title: 22 (Check Your Progress): What happens to the primary current if the secondary of the Figure 15 step-up transformer is short-circuited?

answer.html: A short circuit has almost no resistance, so the secondary current becomes very large, and the transformer must supply a large amount of power. Power in equals power out (𝑉<sub>𝑝</sub>𝐼<sub>𝑝</sub>= 𝑉<sub>𝑠</sub>𝐼<sub>𝑠</sub>), so the primary current rises as well, by the turns ratio: 𝐼<sub>𝑝</sub>= 𝐼<sub>𝑠</sub>(𝑁<sub>𝑠</sub>/ 𝑁<sub>𝑝</sub>) for a step-up transformer. The large primary current can overheat and damage the windings or blow a fuse or trip a breaker.

check.html: The same thing happens in a motor that is stalled: big current when nothing opposes it.

items.title: 23 (Check Your Progress, Critical Thinking): Would permanent magnets make good transformer cores?

answer.html: No. A transformer core has to follow the primary current's alternating field, magnetizing and demagnetizing quickly and in both directions. A permanent magnet is already strongly magnetized and resists changes in its magnetization, so it would carry the changing field poorly and waste energy as heat when its magnetization is forced to reverse. A soft iron core, which is easily magnetized and demagnetized, is used instead.

check.html: The core's job is to concentrate and carry the changing flux from primary to secondary.
